questions.q: In NIST SP 800-207's reference architecture, which component actually runs the trust algorithm and outputs the grant/deny/revoke decision?
options: The Policy Enforcement Point (PEP)
The Continuous Diagnostics and Mitigation (CDM) system
The Policy Engine (PE)
The identity provider's directory service alone
questions.explain: The Policy Engine runs the trust algorithm against policy and contextual inputs and outputs the actual grant/deny/revoke decision for a subject/resource pair.

questions.q: What does NIST group the Policy Engine and Policy Administrator together as?
options: The Policy Decision Point (PDP)
The Continuous Diagnostics and Mitigation (CDM) system
The Policy Enforcement Point (PEP)
The identity and access management (IAM) plane
questions.explain: NIST's own diagram groups the PE and PA together as the Policy Decision Point — the "brain" that decides and issues session credentials — separate from the PEP.

questions.q: What is the Policy Administrator's (PA) specific job, as distinct from the Policy Engine's?
options: It collects threat intelligence feeds for the SIEM
It acts on the PE's decision: establishing or shutting down the communication path, and generating/managing the session-specific token or credential
It performs the actual network packet inspection at the firewall
It owns the long-term, permanent device inventory
questions.explain: The PA doesn't decide — it carries out what the PE already decided, by establishing or ending the session and issuing the credential the subject will use.

questions.q: Why does NIST keep the Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) architecturally separate from the Policy Decision Point (PE + PA)?
options: Because the PEP needs more processing power than the PDP
Because the PEP must always run in a different cloud region than the PDP
Because NIST requires every component to be made by a different vendor
Because it separates deciding and issuing credentials from the component that physically sits on the data path and continuously enables, monitors, or terminates the connection
questions.explain: The PEP is the gate on the actual data path between subject and resource; it enforces what the PDP decided but never makes the decision itself.

questions.q: Which real-world control does this lesson map most closely onto the role of a Policy Enforcement Point (PEP)?
options: A ZTNA gateway, SASE edge, or AWS Verified Access endpoint sitting on the connection path
A SIEM dashboard used for after-the-fact investigation
An HR system storing employee records
A backup and disaster-recovery job scheduler
questions.explain: A ZTNA gateway, SASE edge, or AWS Verified Access endpoint behaves like a PEP — it sits directly on the connection path, granting or cutting access per the decision it's handed.
